title: Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis
formal: Does there exist a constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) such that, for every fixed integer \(a\ge1\), a uniform bounded-error randomized word-RAM algorithm computes the min-plus convolution of any two length-\(n\) integer arrays with entries in \([-n^{a},n^{a}]\) in \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\) worst-case time?
why: A central fine-grained hypothesis supporting quadratic barriers in knapsack and dynamic programming.
status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. The ICALP 2026 paper still states the unrestricted min-plus convolution hypothesis, records a subpolynomial unrestricted speedup, and proves faster results for monotone bounded-range inputs. No fixed-saving algorithm or unconditional impossibility proof for this explicit integer formulation was located. Source proofs were not independently audited.
review_note: Completed individual review against P versus NP on 13 September 2026; see research/card-completion-20260913/reviews.jsonl.

progress.text: Convolution algorithms exploit pair-sum structure without establishing a fixed exponent improvement for general min-plus convolution.
Deterministic faster algorithms handle the monotone structured variant; they do not settle arbitrary polynomially bounded arrays.

category_assignment.reason: The fixed polynomial exponent improvement is a fine-grained complexity target.

definitions: For \(n\ge2\), input arrays \(A=(a_{0},\ldots,a_{n-1})\) and \(B=(b_{0},\ldots,b_{n-1})\) are explicitly listed. Output all \(2n-1\) integers \(c_{k}=\min\{a_{i}+b_{j}:0\le i,j<n,\ i+j=k\}\), for \(0\le k\le2n-2\). Inputs need not be sorted or monotone. Use a uniform word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_{2}(n+2)\rceil\), for a fixed positive integer \(d\) chosen with the algorithm and large enough for its addresses and input values. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), and integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword computation is charged by its component instructions. The fixed finite program receives no advice or precomputed tables; all initialization, preprocessing and output writes count. Randomness consists of independent uniform random words, each generated at unit cost. On every input, the whole output must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\). The time bound holds for every random execution, including unsuccessful ones. The exponent saving \(\varepsilon\) is common to all fixed magnitude exponents \(a\); the program, word-size constant and hidden time constant may depend on \(a\). Signed entries and exact output sums use a constant number of words.

context_blocks.text: Min-plus convolution combines two cost profiles: entry \(c_k\) is the cheapest way to split the total index \(k\) between them. For \(A=(3,1)\) and \(B=(4,2)\), the output is \((7,5,3)\). The middle entry compares two different splits, while an endpoint has only one. All output positions are required simultaneously.

The direct computation checks every pair of input entries, producing a quadratic amount of work for a linear-size output. Unlike ordinary convolution, replacing sums of products by minima of sums changes the algebraic operation. The hypothesis is a computational barrier for this exact cost-combination primitive.

The 2026 paper records an unrestricted upper bound \(n^2/2^{\Theta(\sqrt{\log n})}\), obtained from earlier results. This is an improvement over quadratic time, but its exponent saving tends to zero with input length. The requested algorithm must save a fixed positive exponent, not merely a growing subpolynomial factor.

The same paper gives \(n^{1.5+o(1)}\) deterministic time when the arrays are monotone and their values obey the specified bounded-range condition. Neither monotonicity nor that special linear range is assumed by this card. Structured convolution is therefore a restricted positive result rather than an unrestricted resolution.

The established hypothesis name predicts a negative answer to the displayed algorithm-existence question. The card fixes a precise polynomially bounded integer formulation: one exponent saving works for every fixed magnitude exponent \(a\), while the implementation and constants may depend on \(a\). There is no claim about arbitrary real-number inputs or bit lengths growing faster than \(O(\log n)\).

The probability guarantee is for the entire output on each fixed input. A small error probability for each entry separately would not automatically give that guarantee for the full array. Likewise, average performance over an input distribution is different from the worst-case time and per-input correctness requirements.

answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that some fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) permits the stated family of uniform algorithms for every fixed magnitude exponent \(a\), with worst-case time and whole-output success guarantees, or prove the logical negation in Lean. In the negation, every proposed saving \(\varepsilon\) fails for at least one fixed \(a\), allowing all permitted algorithms and their constants. Neither a conditional hardness implication nor a theorem for monotone inputs proves that negation.

formulation_history.previous_formal: Is there an \(\varepsilon >0\) and a randomized bounded-error algorithm computing the min-plus convolution of two length-n arrays of polynomially bounded integers in \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\) time on a word RAM?
formulation_history.reason: Completes the existing TCS-6598 integer-word target, including output indexing, magnitude quantifiers, bounded error and worst-case cost. The established hypothesis title is retained; the yes/no statement asks whether its algorithmic negation holds.

sentences: Min-plus convolution returns the minimum sum of two array entries for each possible sum of their indices.
The input arrays contain polynomially bounded integers and need not be monotone.
The question asks for a fixed improvement in the quadratic running-time exponent.
Bounded-error randomization is allowed and every output entry must be correct simultaneously.
Faster algorithms for monotone instances do not settle this unrestricted fine-grained barrier.
